title_options: Where Your Body's Energy Actually Goes 🔋

share.myth: Sitting still uses almost no energy.
share.truth: Even at rest a person turns over about 40 kg of ATP a day, spent on muscles, ion pumps that keep nerves ready, and building proteins; nearly all of it is remade by ATP synthase (Tymoczko, Berg & Stryer; Watt et al. 2010, PNAS).
share.line: Even sitting still, you spend about forty kilograms of ATP a day, and tiny turbines rebuild every bit of it.

facts: Tymoczko, Berg & Stryer, Biochemistry: A Short Course (3rd ed.): a resting human uses about 40 kg of ATP in 24 hours.
ATP powers muscle contraction, the sodium-potassium pump that keeps nerve cells ready to fire, and protein synthesis (standard biochemistry textbooks).
Watt IN et al. 2010, PNAS 107:16823: ATP synthase rotates about 100 times per second, making 3 ATP per turn.
description: Even sitting still you spend about 40 kg of ATP a day, on muscles, nerves and building proteins, and tiny turbines rebuild all of it. Chapter 7 of our book The Tiny Turbine That Powers Your Body. #shorts #biology #science #ATP
sources: Tymoczko, Berg & Stryer, Biochemistry: A Short Course, 3rd ed. (ATP turnover and uses); Watt et al. 2010, PNAS 107:16823 (ATP synthase).

scenes.narration: Even sitting perfectly still, your cells burn through about forty kilograms of ATP a day.
Where does it all go? First, your muscles. Every pull of every fibre spends ATP.
Then your nerves. Pumps spend ATP to keep every nerve cell ready to fire.
Then building. Every new protein your cells make is paid for in ATP.
And your heart and brain never stop asking for it, even while you sleep.
All of it is rebuilt by turbines in your mitochondria, spinning about a hundred times a second.
Even sitting still, you spend about forty kilograms of ATP a day, and tiny turbines rebuild every bit of it.
So what do you think happens to all those turbines when you start to run?
